summary: Explains how to run LSP ping and traceroute across MPLS tunnels and stitched label switched paths, which RFC 4379 could not fully check. It deprecates the Downstream Mapping TLV in favor of a new one. It updates RFC 4379 and was replaced by RFC 8029.

plainLanguage.summary: Checking a path through a tunnel is hard, like following a road that dives underground. This gives routers a better way to trace the whole path. It was later replaced by RFC 8029.

questions: how does lsp traceroute work over mpls tunnels
what is the downstream detailed mapping tlv
what is a fec stack change sub-tlv
subtitle: How LSP ping and traceroute follow a path through MPLS tunnels and stitched label switched paths.

tldr.problem: RFC 4379 traceroute cannot properly validate or follow a path that goes through other MPLS tunnels or through stitched LSPs, because the tracing router is not told when the FEC being traced changes.
tldr.mechanism: A new Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV with sub-TLVs lets each router report the labels and any FEC pushes or pops, so the ingress can keep an accurate FEC stack for each path. The old Downstream Mapping TLV is deprecated.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6424 is a Standards Track update to RFC 4379. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 8029 and updated by RFC 7537.

facts.label: Sub-TLV types
facts.value: 1 Multipath data, 2 Label stack, 3 FEC stack change

today: RFC 6424 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8029 and updated by RFC 7537. It updated RFC 4379.

sections.title: What This Document Changes
sections.content:
LSP ping, defined in RFC 4379, includes a traceroute mode with FEC validation (checking that the packet is on the path for the Forwarding Equivalency Class being traced) and Equal Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) path discovery. Those mechanisms are not enough when the traced FEC crosses one or more MPLS tunnels, or when LSP stitching (RFC 5150) is in use.

RFC 6424 describes how a traceroute request can traverse tunnels with correct FEC and label validation. It does this by deprecating the Downstream Mapping TLV from RFC 4379 and introducing a more extensible TLV that carries detailed information. The document updates RFC 4379.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking a road through a tunnel needs better signs than the old ones had. This memo puts up new signs that work in tunnels too.

sections.title: Why Plain LSP Traceroute Falls Short
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example of an LDP LSP running over an RSVP tunnel across routers A, B, C, D and E. When the trace reaches router C, which is a pure RSVP node and does not run LDP, C receives the echo request with two labels but only one FEC in the Target FEC stack. It cannot do a complete FEC validation, so it just forwards based on the incoming label. The RFC says that ignoring FEC validation defeats the purpose of control-plane validation.

The same problem applies to hierarchical tunnels and to stitched LSPs, where two or more LSP segments, possibly signaled by different protocols, are joined. When a FEC stack change happens at a stitching router, the ingress has no way to learn of it, so the next router knows nothing about the FEC being traced.

As a result, the RFC 4379 procedures do not let the ingress know that tunneling happened, trace the path of the tunnel, or trace the path of stitched LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: If the trail switches roads inside a tunnel and nobody tells the tracker, the tracker gets lost. The routers need a way to say, we just changed roads.

sections.title: The Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV
sections.content:
The new Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV (DDMAP) has type 20. It may be included in an MPLS echo request, and only one may appear in a request. Its presence asks for DDMAP objects in the echo reply. A replying router that is the destination of the FEC SHOULD NOT include one; otherwise it SHOULD include one for each interface over which the FEC could be forwarded.

The fixed part holds the MTU, Address Type, DS Flags, the downstream address and downstream interface address, a Return Code, a Return Subcode and a Sub-tlv Length. Variable and optional fields from the old TLV are now sub-TLVs, which makes the format extensible.

The FEC stack change sub-TLV is the key addition. A router MUST include it when the downstream node in the echo reply has a different FEC stack than the one in the request. It carries an operation type (1 Push or 2 Pop), a remote peer address and, for a push, the FEC itself. A Nil FEC may be used to hide details of a pushed FEC.

Two new return codes are defined: 14, which says the return code is per DDMAP and is required when there are multiple downstreams (ECMP or P2MP), and 15, "Label switched with FEC change", which a stitching point SHOULD use. Code 15 MUST NOT be used if no FEC stack change sub-TLV is present.

The rules for FEC stack change sub-TLVs are strict. A push MUST NOT be followed by a pop, one or more pops MAY be followed by pushes, one sub-TLV is included per FEC change, and a splice is a pop followed by a push. A DDMAP containing only a single pop is equivalent to an IS_EGRESS (return code 3) for the outermost FEC.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router now fills in a detailed note: here are the next labels, and here is where I added or removed a road. The note has pieces that can be added later, so it can grow.

sections.title: How Routers and the Ingress Behave
sections.content:
A transit node that starts a new tunnel SHOULD add one FEC stack change sub-TLV with a push operation for each new tunnel, and fill in the remote peer address or set the address type to Unspecified if it does not know it. The Label stack sub-TLV MUST contain one extra label per pushed FEC. If the tunnel is a transparent pipe whose trace will not expire in the middle, the node SHOULD NOT add the sub-TLV.

For stitched LSPs, a stitching node SHOULD report a pop for the old FEC and a push for the new one, and set return code 15. A node that wants to hide its tunnel SHOULD push a Nil FEC. If the outermost FEC in the target FEC stack is a Nil FEC, transit and egress nodes MUST skip target FEC validation completely.

The ingress keeps a FEC stack per path being traced. It applies the pops and pushes from each reply to that path only, and the next echo request uses the updated stack. The RFC gives pseudo-code that drops the reply if a pop follows a push, if a pop is attempted on an empty stack, or if the stack ends up empty.

Because new FECs may have been added, a return code 3 reply may be for an added FEC rather than the original. The ingress checks the depth of the target FEC sent. If it differs from the depth being traced, it pops an entry and resends with the same TTL, repeating until it gets a non-egress reply or all added FECs are popped. This lets the ingress map the hierarchical LSP structure.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router sends traffic into a new tunnel, it says so and tells which tunnel. The tracker writes this down, and when it hears we are at the end of a tunnel, it steps back out to the bigger road and keeps going.

sections.title: Working With the Old Downstream Mapping TLV
sections.content:
RFC 6424 deprecates the Downstream Mapping TLV, and applications should use the DDMAP instead. For routers that do not support the new TLV, the RFC sets these rules:

  • The two TLVs MUST never be sent together in the same echo request or reply.
  • If a request with a DDMAP gets return code 2 ("One or more of the TLVs was not understood"), the sender MAY resend the request with the old TLV.
  • If a request contains the old TLV, the reply MUST NOT contain a DDMAP.
  • An intermediate router that forwards echo requests MUST NOT forward a request or reply with a DDMAP if it does not support that TLV itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old routers only understand the old notes. So the rule is to never mix old and new notes in one message, and to fall back to the old style if a router is confused.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists two security points. An operator who wants to prevent tracing inside a tunnel can use the Pipe Model (RFC 3443) by not propagating the MPLS TTL into the outer tunnel, so trace packets will not expire there. An operator who does not want to expose details of the outer LSP can use the Nil FEC, which keeps the trace progressing while the transit nodes still do some minimal validation. Security considerations from RFC 4379 also apply.

IANA assigned TLV type 20 for the DDMAP, created a registry for its sub-TLV types (valid range 0-65535) with sub-types 1 Multipath data, 2 Label stack and 3 FEC stack change, and assigned return codes 14 and 15.
sections.plainLanguage: If a network owner wants to keep the inside of a tunnel private, they can make the trace skip over it or give it a plain label instead of the real name.
